headline: A new pill may cure one kind of high blood pressure

sources.title: New drug could be cure for common cause of high blood pressure (The Guardian)
New treatment may cure common hormonal cause of high blood pressure (Queen Mary University of London)
New Drug Strategy May Put Hormone-Driven Hypertension Into Lasting Remission (Inside Precision Medicine)

chunks.text: A new [[daily pill]] may cure one common cause of high blood pressure. The [[small study]] was published in the New England Journal of Medicine on November 7, 2026. Patients took the pill for 6 to 12 months and then stopped. Their blood pressure {{went down}} during [[treatment]]. Up to two years later, the [[benefit]] had still not {{worn off}}. Just under a quarter of them {{came off}} all blood pressure medicine.

verbs.wrong: To be checked many times a day
verbs.why: Gas prices go down in the winter. My fever goes down when I rest. The patients' blood pressure went down while they took the pill.

verbs.correct: To slowly become weaker and end
verbs.wrong: To cause a mild side effect
verbs.why: Pain medicine wears off after a few hours. The effect of my morning coffee wears off by noon. Up to two years after the patients stopped, the benefit of the pill had still not worn off.

verbs.wrong: To change to a new doctor
verbs.why: Some people come off sleeping pills slowly, with help from a doctor. My uncle wants to come off his pain medicine soon. Just under a quarter of the patients came off all their blood pressure medicine.

chunks.text: More than a billion people have high blood pressure. In 5 to 10 percent of cases, the cause is small [[growths]] on two [[glands]] above the kidneys. They are not cancer. Glands are organs that make [[hormones]], [[chemical messages]] in the blood. The growths {{pump out}} too much of one hormone. It tells the kidneys to {{hold on to}} salt. That {{pushes up}} blood pressure. The usual treatment is [[surgery]] to {{take out}} the [[affected]] gland.

verbs.correct: To make a large amount of something
verbs.wrong: To slowly grow larger in size
verbs.why: That factory pumps out thousands of cars a year. Our old heater pumps out a lot of heat. The growths pump out too much of one hormone.

verbs.correct: To keep something instead of losing it
verbs.wrong: To measure the amount of something
verbs.why: A sponge holds on to water. Some people hold on to old clothes for years. The hormone tells the kidneys to hold on to salt.

verbs.wrong: To make a person feel tired
verbs.why: Bad weather pushes up the price of fruit. Stress often pushes up your heart rate. Holding on to salt pushes up blood pressure.

verbs.correct: To remove a body part during surgery
verbs.wrong: To study the body with a camera
verbs.why: Surgeons take out the appendix when it gets infected. A dentist takes out wisdom teeth in a short surgery. The usual treatment is surgery to take out the affected gland.

chunks.text: A high blood pressure expert at Queen Mary University of London led the study. It included 14 patients at eight [[medical centers]] in the U.S. Doctors {{followed up}} with them for up to two years. On average, their blood pressure was 25 points lower. A [[blood test]] for the extra hormone showed levels 99 percent lower than before treatment. The lead researcher says the results {{back up}} an idea from a 2005 [[experiment]] in mice.

verbs.correct: To contact someone again to see how they are
verbs.wrong: To send a patient to a new hospital
verbs.why: The nurse follows up with me a week after each visit. Good doctors follow up with patients after surgery. Doctors followed up with the patients for up to two years.

verbs.correct: To show that an idea may be true
verbs.wrong: To repeat a test on new patients
verbs.why: Photos back up her story about the accident. Many studies back up the advice to walk every day. The results back up an idea from a 2005 experiment in mice.

chunks.text: The idea is that the pill may cause the cells that make the extra hormone to {{die off}}. The study was small and had no [[comparison group]] of patients who did not get the pill. A Harvard professor who worked on the study said it is too early to call anyone [[cured]]. Queen Mary has {{set up}} a [[larger trial]] with about 30 patients. It will try to {{find out}} if the pill really cures the condition.

verbs.correct: To die one by one until few are left
verbs.wrong: To move to another part of the body
verbs.why: Many plants die off in a cold winter. Some fish die off when the water gets too warm. The lead researcher thinks the pill may cause the cells that make the extra hormone to die off.

verbs.correct: To plan and start something new
verbs.why: Many schools set up a club for new students. The city sets up a free clinic every summer. Queen Mary has set up a larger trial with about 30 patients.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.wrong: To share news with other people
verbs.why: Students find out their test scores online. A blood test helps doctors find out what is wrong. The larger trial will try to find out if the pill really cures the condition.

mainIdea.s: In a small study, a daily pill lowered blood pressure caused by growths that make too much of a hormone. The effect lasted up to two years after patients stopped, but more tests are needed.
mainIdea.why: Up to two years later, the benefit had still not worn off. The study was small, so Queen Mary has set up a larger trial.

mainIdea.s: A large study proved that a new pill cures high blood pressure in most people with these gland growths. Because of the results, doctors in the U.S. no longer remove the glands with surgery.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the study had only 14 patients and did not prove a cure. A Harvard professor said it is too early to call anyone cured.

mainIdea.s: A new report says that eating less salt can lower blood pressure for millions of adults. Health officials now want food companies to use less salt in bread, canned soup and frozen snacks.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a daily pill for people whose gland growths pump out too much of a hormone. It is not about salt in food.

tf.s: In the study, the benefit did not wear off when patients stopped the pill.
tf.why: Their blood pressure was still lower up to two years after their last pill.

tf.s: Every patient in the study came off all blood pressure medicine.
tf.why: Just under a quarter of the patients came off all their blood pressure medicine, not every patient.

tf.s: The hormone makes the kidneys lose more salt than usual.
tf.why: It tells the kidneys to hold on to salt, and that pushes up blood pressure.

tf.s: Small growths on the glands pump out too much of one hormone.
tf.why: The growths pump out too much of a hormone, and this causes 5 to 10 percent of high blood pressure cases.

tf.s: The study included a large number of patients.
tf.why: It was small, with only 14 patients, so a larger trial will try to find out more.

tf.s: Queen Mary has set up a larger trial of the pill.
tf.why: The new trial, with about 30 patients, will try to find out if the pill really cures the condition.

lines.text: Did you see the news about the new blood pressure pill? It's [[good news for a change]].
I saw the headline. What's so special about it?
Patients took it every day for 6 to 12 months, and their blood pressure {{went down}}.
Lots of pills do that, though.
Sure, but this time the benefit didn't {{wear off}} after they stopped. It lasted as long as two years.
And just under a quarter of them {{came off}} all blood pressure medicine.
People with small growths on two glands near the kidneys. The growths {{pump out}} too much of one hormone.
It makes the kidneys {{hold on to}} salt, and that {{pushes up}} blood pressure.
So what do doctors usually do now?
Wouldn't you rather take a pill than have surgery?
[[You bet]]. But the study only had 14 patients. The headline says "may," and that's [[the key word]].
So a real cure is still [[a ways off]]?
Probably. A larger trial will try to {{find out}} if the pill really cures it.
I hope the new results {{back up}} this first study.
